advisor.summary: A health reimbursement arrangement is an employer-funded plan that reimburses employees' medical care: the corporation deducts the payments under §162(a), the employee excludes them under §105(b) and §106(a), and FICA never applies. The C corporation is the clean chassis because its owner-employee is simply an employee — §1372 denies >2% S corporation shareholders the same exclusion. The controlling hazard is the ACA market reforms: a standalone HRA covering two or more employees must integrate with group coverage or fit a sanctioned design, on pain of the §4980D excise at $100 per affected individual per day; a plan with fewer than two current-employee participants is exempt. Advisory-only — the benefit turns on entity structure and actual medical spend, so it is quantified in plan design rather than modeled from return inputs.
mechanics: The corporation adopts a written reimbursement plan; payments for medical care described in §213(d) for the employee, spouse, and dependents are deductible under §162(a) and excluded from income and FICA wages under §105(b) and §106(a).

A C-corp owner-employee participates like any other employee — the double-tax structure that usually penalizes C corporations works in the owner's favor here, turning family medical costs into corporate deductions with no shareholder-level income.
Pass-through owners are locked out: §1372 treats >2% S corporation shareholders as partners, so their reimbursements land on the W-2 and route through §162(l) instead of being excluded.

A standalone HRA covering two or more current employees violates the ACA market reforms unless it is integrated with group coverage or structured as a QSEHRA, ICHRA, or excepted-benefit HRA; a plan with fewer than two current-employee participants is exempt under §9831(a)(2), which is why owner-only C corporations implement this with little friction.
Self-insured nondiscrimination under §105(h) still applies: an HRA that favors highly compensated individuals as to eligibility or benefits makes the HCI's excess reimbursements taxable.

authority.note: Excludes employer reimbursements of medical expenses of the employee, spouse, and dependents from income.
Excludes the employer-provided coverage itself from the employee's income.
Grounds the corporate deduction for reimbursements and plan costs as ordinary compensation expense.
Nondiscrimination rules for self-insured plans; discriminatory excess reimbursements are taxable to highly compensated individuals.
The reason S corporations fail here: >2% shareholders are treated as partners for fringe-benefit purposes.
The market-reform analysis: a standalone HRA covering two or more employees must integrate with group coverage or fit an excepted design.
The excise tax — $100 per affected individual per day — that enforces the market-reform rules.
Exempts plans with fewer than two current-employee participants from the market reforms.
Defines the medical care an HRA may reimburse tax-free.

requirements: A C corporation employing the owner as a bona fide W-2 employee.
A written plan document — covered class, annual limit, substantiation procedure — adopted before the first reimbursement is paid.
A documented ACA compliance path: the one-participant exemption, integration with group coverage, or a sanctioned design.
Receipts or EOBs substantiating each reimbursement before it is paid.
§105(h) testing whenever the plan is self-insured and the corporation employs a broader workforce.
risks: The dominant exposure is the §4980D excise — $100 per affected individual per day, $36,500 per individual per year — for a standalone design that fails the market reforms; Notice 2013-54 controls, which is why the compliance path is settled before the plan is adopted, not after.
§105(h) discrimination turns the owner's excess reimbursements into taxable income when a broader workforce is excluded.

Unsubstantiated or non-§213(d) reimbursements forfeit the exclusion, and a corporation whose only substance is paying the family's medical bills invites constructive-dividend recharacterization of the entire arrangement.
Never let the HRA drive entity choice on its own — double taxation on remaining C-corp earnings can swamp the health benefit; run the full entity comparison.
Every new hire shifts the plan's legal posture: the one-participant exemption disappears the day a second employee becomes eligible.
stateNotes: Conformity: states that start from federal AGI or federal taxable income conform to both the corporate deduction and the employee exclusion, so no separate state filing position is needed in conforming states.
PTET: none — the sponsor is a C corporation, so no pass-through entity tax interaction arises.

Missouri: conforms — the deduction flows through the Missouri corporate return's federal-taxable-income starting point (RSMo §143.431), and the exclusion never enters Missouri AGI under RSMo §143.121.
reviewChecklist: Written plan and board resolution signed and dated before any reimbursement.
ACA compliance path documented for the current participant count.
Substantiation process running — receipts or EOBs collected before payment, log kept current.
§105(h) analysis current against the census; owner-only status confirmed wherever the exemption is relied on.
Any savings figure presented ties to actual family medical spend, not the plan cap.

client.teaser: Your corporation can pay your family's medical bills — a deduction for it, tax-free money for you.
client.headline: Let your company pay the medical bills your family already has
plainEnglish: A regular C corporation can adopt a formal plan that pays employees back for medical costs — doctor visits, prescriptions, dental, vision, deductibles. The company deducts every payment. The employee owes no tax on them.

Here is the key. If you own the company and work in it, you are one of those employees. Bills your family pays anyway, with money that was already taxed, can instead be paid by the company with money that is never taxed.

Health-care law sets strict rules for these plans, and the penalty for a sloppy one is steep. So the paperwork comes first and the payments second. We design the plan, put the documents in place, and keep the records clean.
client.analogy: Think of it as a standing discount on every medical bill, equal to your tax rate. The money that pays the doctor never passes through your taxable income.
benefits: Family medical costs turn into company deductions
Reimbursements come to you free of income and payroll tax
Covers what insurance skips — deductibles, dental, vision
Works again every year the plan stays in place
steps: WE confirm your setup qualifies and choose the compliant plan design.
WE put the written plan in place before any money moves.
YOU turn in receipts; the company pays you back.
WE tie out the plan and the deduction at year-end.
clientCommitments: Send a receipt or insurance statement with every request — no receipt, no payment
Tell us before you hire — a second employee changes the plan rules
Pay reimbursements from the company account, never as informal transfers

annualMaintenance: Annual §105(h) re-test whenever the census changes
Year-end reconciliation of reimbursements, substantiation, and the Form 1120 deduction
deliverables: Written HRA plan document and adopting board resolution
